analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the federal estate and gift taxes was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in January 2013 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the federal estate tax — the tax on very large inheritances when someone dies — as well as the gift tax and a related tax on transfers that skip a generation. It was introduced by Representative Tim Griffin of Arkansas with two cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates and the wealthy families doing large lifetime gifts. The federal estate tax applies only to estates above a high exemption threshold, so repeal would concentrate its benefit on the largest fortunes. Heirs to family farms and small businesses above the threshold would also gain, as would estate-planning professionals whose services center on minimizing these taxes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely, applied retroactively to the date of enactment.
Supporters brand it the "Death Tax Repeal Act," arguing that heirs should not pay tax on inherited farms and businesses.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury would lose the revenue the estate and gift taxes raise from the largest estates — money that would otherwise come from taxpayers generally, adding to deficits or requiring other taxes to make up the difference. Ordinary families, who rarely owe these taxes, gain essentially nothing but share the fiscal cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals not just the estate tax but the gift tax as well, opening a route for transferring large fortunes to heirs tax-free during life as well as at death.
Eliminating the tax removes federal revenue that would otherwise come from the largest estates, meaning the cost is spread through higher deficits or other taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The estate tax applies to only a small share of the largest estates, so repeal would have produced little direct benefit for most families but a substantial tax cut for very wealthy heirs, offset by higher deficits or other taxes. For a bill framed as helping family farms and small businesses, the actual distribution of benefits would have run heavily toward the largest fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history consists of its introduction on January 4, 2013 and its referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 without further action.
The bill would have repealed the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, which apply only to the largest estates and large lifetime gifts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury, in the short run, is the direct beneficiary: the estate and gift taxes remained in place for the largest estates. Working people were largely unaffected either way, since the tax rarely applies to estates of their size.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; estates kept paying

for.name: Rep. Tim Griffin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes on January 4, 2013.

for.name: 2 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors, both Republicans.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and large estate holders
industries.note: Heirs to the largest fortunes would owe no estate tax and no gift tax on transfers, the biggest beneficiaries of the bill. Ordinary people are largely unaffected because most estates fall below the taxable threshold.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: With transfer taxes repealed, the demand for estate planning shifts but the wealthiest clients keep more; the industry's core product of minimizing estate taxes would change rather than disappear.

industries.industry: Family farms and small business owners
industries.note: A recurring argument for repeal is that heirs should not have to sell farms or businesses to pay the tax; in practice the very largest estates capture most of the benefit, and ordinary taxpayers were already largely exempt.
